ritual_roles: Supreme creator, divine ancestor, and eternal patron of the Gaddi people. Gaddis consider themselves 'Shivvanshi' (lineage of Shiva) and believe Lord Shiva resides on Mount Manimahesh Kailash wearing a woollen chola like a shepherd.
traditional_offerings: Consecrated ram (Khadu), sweet roat, rice pulao, un-boiled milk, wild mountain flowers (dhoop).
source_citation: Chakraborty (2024), Section: Religious Life; Shashi (1977), pp. 45-52; Dar & Sheikh (2022), p. 247
description: Lord Shiva is the central divine figure of Gaddi existence. In Gaddi oral tradition, Shiva is neither abstract nor distant; he is conceived of as an intimate shepherd elder who watches over his people and flocks across high mountain passes.
regional_distinctions: While Shiva is worshipped across India, Gaddi Shaivism is unique in its pastoral, egalitarian theology, the centrality of the Shiv Nawala ritual, and the veneration of Manimahesh peak as an un-climbed sacred mountain.

ritual_roles: The supreme minister/general (Wazir) of Lord Shiva and the foremost guardian deity of shepherds, flocks, and high mountain passes. Propitiated before leading sheep across dangerous alpine ridges like the Kugti and Chobia passes.
traditional_offerings: Iron tridents (trishul), brass bells, coconuts, red flags (dhaja), incense, consecrated he-goat.
source_citation: Shashi (1977), pp. 52-55; Chakraborty (2024), Section: Shepherd Guardian Deities; Nirmohi, p. 89
description: Kelang Wazir is an exclusively Gaddi pastoral deity. His principal historic shrine is at Kugti village near the foot of the Kugti pass leading into Lahaul. Gaddi shepherds believe that no flock can safely traverse the high snowfields without Kelang's blessing.
regional_distinctions: Specific to Gaddi transhumance routes in Chamba, Kangra, and border pastures with Lahaul and Jammu.

ritual_roles: Pastoral warrior-saint and protector deity invoked against snakebite, venomous scorpions, and cattle illnesses.
traditional_offerings: Milk, sweet rot bread, vermillion, flags, grain offerings.
source_citation: PLSI Vol. 12 (2014), p. 125; Chakraborty (2024), Section: Folk Deities
description: Guga Jaharveer is revered throughout the Western Himalayan foothills. Traveling Gaddi bards sing heroic epics of Guga during the monsoon season to ensure that shepherds sleeping outdoors on rocky ridges remain unharmed by poisonous snakes.
regional_distinctions: Shared with wider Pahari, Punjabi, and Rajasthani pastoral communities, but Gaddi worship features distinct musical ballad styles.

ritual_roles: Ancient patron goddess guarding the southern approaches of Bharmaur. The 8th-century deodar wood temple founded by King Meru Varman is an architectural and spiritual landmark for Gaddis.
traditional_offerings: Brass lamps, silk scarves, sweet prasad, vermillion.
description: Sandhya Devi represents the divinity of twilight. Her temple features intricate post-Gupta wooden carvings and an ancient bronze idol sculpted by master craftsman Gugga in c. 750 CE.
regional_distinctions: Rooted specifically in the heritage of Bharmaur / Chhatrari.

ritual_roles: Fierce protective goddess of the ancient Gaddi capital Bharmaur; worshipped for health, fertility, and community safety.
traditional_offerings: Incense, holy water, coconut, red cloth.
description: Housed within the sacred Chaurasi complex, the temple of Lakshana Devi dates back to c. 680 CE and is considered one of the oldest surviving wooden temples in the Himalayas.
regional_distinctions: Bharmaur heritage landmark revered by all Gaddi clans.

associated_locations: Household shrines in Kangra and Jammu
ritual_roles: Fierce avatar invoked for domestic protection against evil spirits, witchcraft, and sudden illness. Represented by unhewn stones or brass amulets worn by Gaddi men.
traditional_offerings: Walnuts, red flowers, sweet roat bread.
source_citation: Chakraborty (2024), Section: Folk Deities; Nirmohi, p. 112
description: Narsingh is venerated intimately within Gaddi homes as a household protector who ensures that no malign energies afflict children or livestock.
regional_distinctions: Prominent throughout Western Himalayan folk religion.

associated_locations: Clan shrines across all Gaddi villages
ritual_roles: Spirits of ancestors who died without male offspring. Propitiated with stone tablets (mohra) carved with stylized human figures placed near natural water springs or field boundaries.
traditional_offerings: Rice, cooked pulses, milk, oblations of spring water.
source_citation: Shashi (1977), pp. 60-61; Chandar (2024), Section: Ancestral Rites
description: Ancestral veneration forms an indispensable pillar of Gaddi life, ensuring familial continuity and spiritual balance across generations.
regional_distinctions: Distinct Gaddi form of ancestor propitiation using water-side mohra stones.

ritual_roles: Guardian of natural springs (baoli/naun), mountain streams, and underground water sources. Honored to guarantee abundant water and rain for pastures.
traditional_offerings: Fresh cow milk, saffron, spring flowers, flour dough snakes.
source_citation: Dar & Sheikh (2022), p. 247; Nirmohi, Duggar Ka Itihas, pp. 88-92
description: In the Jammu hills and Bharmaur, Nag deities are intimately linked with spring water purity. Gaddi shepherds maintain strict cleanliness around water shrines in their pastures.
regional_distinctions: Central to Bhadarwah and Western Pahari spiritual geography.
